Beware Of Narks Online Trying To Entrap You Into Selling Them Weed – Important!

Why Fight Crime When There Are Drugs Online?

September 30, 1999

From http://www.thestandard.com
The Newsmagazine of the Internet economy

The mainstream press loves stories about illicit doings on the Web. Of course, so do we – but we'd prefer to see a bit more depth than we'd find on "Hard Copy." A group of articles this weekend about the cyber drug trade shows that reporters can be just as shallow when covering drugs on the Web as when they write about prohibition's offline discontents.
(Marijuananews note: Notice the use of the word "prohibition!")

Both the San Jose Mercury News and Reuters reported that eBay shut down an auction for 500 pounds of marijuana that was said to be from Holland. When it was stopped, the bidding had reached $10 million. No one's sure whether the auction was real or a hoax, but the story underlines the way the amorphous quality of Net borders can help subvert the drug war. Which is not to say that the reporters played that angle.

Rather than throw in the towel on the battle against chemical recreation, the cops have started lurking about chat rooms.

They've taken down villains like 30-year-old ex-cop Rhonda Bankens, who was about to sell a whole ounce of pot to an undercover cop. According to a story on MSNBC, the current cop "developed an online relationship with her and used three weeks of online conversations to coax Bankens to supply him with marijuana."

(Marijuananews note: Three weeks to buy an ounce! What a bizarre waste of police resources. One need not be an anti-prohibitionist to think that this is absurd.)

The article goes on to follow Louisiana narcotics detective Luke Erickson, who, in a state with one of the highest crime rates in the country, "[H]as built a career of infiltrating chat rooms on America Online and arresting those who offer him drugs."

Never mind the fact that online drug-trading is the ultimate victimless crime – as the story itself points out.

"The online trade that cops stumble across is mainly small-time sales for personal use," says the MSNBC tale. "Online drug sellers don't blight neighborhoods by appropriating street corners or abandoned homes. And when they buy, customers don't carry guns or worry about getting mugged."

The section on Erickson has the nauseating subhead "One Soldier's Battle." Apparently it takes a true hero to be a narc in cyberspace.
